ety.text: First attested in 1526; borrowed from Latin ēvacuātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvacuō (“to empty out, evacuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

senses.d: To leave or withdraw from; to quit; to retire from.
ex: The firefighters told us to evacuate the area as the flames approached.

senses.d: To cause (or help) to leave or withdraw from.
ex: The firefighters decided to evacuate all the inhabitants from the street.

senses.d: To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of, including to create a vacuum.
ex: The scientist evacuated the chamber before filling it with nitrogen.

senses.d: To make empty; to deprive.
ex: Evacuate the Scriptures of their most important doctrines.

senses.d: To remove; to eject; to void; to discharge, as the contents of a vessel, or of the bladder or the bowels (to stool).
ex: In the living state, the body is observed to receive aliment; to assimilate a part; to evacuate what is redundant or useless; [...]

senses.d: To make void; to nullify; to vacate.
ex: to evacuate a contract or marriage
it would not evacuate a marriage after cohabitation and actual consummation

grp.label: to move out of an unsafe location into safety

ety.text: Inherited from Old French evacuer, a borrowing from Latin ēvacuāre.

it:evacuare.gl: to evacuate, to empty out, to abandon

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin ēvacuāre (“to empty out; to evacuate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ēvacuō, from vacuus (“empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to lack; empty”).
From Middle English evacuacioun, from Old French evacuation, from Late Latin ēvacuātiō. Equivalent to evacuate + -ion.

senses.d: The act of evacuating; leaving a place in an orderly fashion, especially for safety.
Withdrawal of troops or civils from a town, country, fortress, etc.
The act of emptying, clearing of the contents, or discharging, including creating a vacuum.

Voidance of any matter by the natural passages of the body or by an artificial opening; defecation; urination; also, a diminution of the fluids of an animal body by cathartics, venesection, or other means.
That which is evacuated or discharged; especially, a discharge by stool, urine or other natural means.
ex: The Abſcess being broken an Ulcer is left behind, which may be known by the Evacuation of Matter by Vomit and Stool

senses.d: Abolition; nullification.

grp.label: act of evacuating; leaving a place in an orderly fashion, especially for safety
voidance of matter by natural passages of body

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin ēvacuātiōnem. By surface analysis, evacuar + -ção.
From French évaluation. By surface analysis, evaluate + -ion.

senses.d: An assessment, such as an annual personnel performance review used as the basis for a salary increase or bonus, or a summary of a particular situation.
ex: The result of the semestral evaluation will go towards your final score.

senses.d: A completion of a mathematical operation; a valuation.
Determination of the value of a variable or expression.

ety.text: Latin -ereinflu. Latin -āre Old French -ier Middle French -er French -er French évaluerbor. Spanish evaluar Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ōnem Latin -tiōnemlbor. Spanish -ción Spanish evaluación From evaluar + -ción.

senses.d: To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.
ex: It will take several years to evaluate the material gathered in the survey.
Death is a factor that changes all our views as we are forced to evaluate our worth and what ultimately matters in life.

senses.d: To compute or determine the value of (an expression).
To return or have a specific value.

grp.label: to draw conclusions from by examining

ety.text: Latin -ereinflu. Latin -āre Old French -ier Middle French -er French -er French évaluerbor. Spanish evaluar Borrowed from French évaluer.
From evangelic + -al, from Old French evangelique, from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

senses.d: Pertaining to the doctrines or teachings of the Christian gospel or Christianity in general.
Pertaining to the gospel(s) of the Christian New Testament.
Protestant; specifically Lutheran and Calvinist churches in continental Europe as well as their offshoots in North America.
Pertaining to a movement in Protestant Christianity that stresses personal conversion and the authority of the Bible (evangelicalism).
ex: “They wave their Bibles at passersby, screaming their condemnations,” writes Kurt Eichenwald of evangelical Christians.

senses.d: Pertaining to Islamic groups that are dedicated to dawah and preaching the Quran and sunnah.
Zealously enthusiastic.
A member of an evangelical church.
An advocate of evangelicalism.

grp.label: pertaining to the doctrines or teachings of the Christian gospel or Christianity in general
Pertaining to a movement in Protestant Christianity that stresses personal conversion
